name: Turf toe (first MTP hyperextension sprain)
aliases: plantar plate injury of the hallux

reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Sprain of the plantar capsuloligamentous complex (plantar plate) of the first metatarsophalangeal joint from forced hyperextension of the great toe
Common on hard artificial surfaces ('turf') and in sports involving push-off with the foot fixed in dorsiflexion
The plantar plate, sesamoid complex and collateral ligaments may be injured; severe cases can involve sesamoid fracture, diastasis or dislocation
Presents with pain, swelling and bruising at the first MTP joint and painful, limited toe extension
Graded by severity, with assessment of sesamoid position and joint stability
Radiographs assess sesamoid position and fracture, and MRI best characterises plantar plate and sesamoid injury

Management is graded, with relative rest, protection using stiff-soled footwear or taping to limit dorsiflexion, and progressive rehabilitation; higher grades and structural injury such as sesamoid disruption or plate rupture may need surgery
Inadequately managed injuries can lead to persistent pain, stiffness and hallux deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Turf toe is an injury to the plantar capsuloligamentous complex of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, caused by forced hyperextension (dorsiflexion) of the hallux while the forefoot is fixed on the ground, as in push-off on a hard surface. The plantar plate, the sesamoid apparatus and flexor mechanism, and the collateral ligaments may be stretched or torn; in severe injury there can be sesamoid fracture, retraction or diastasis and joint instability or dislocation. The sesamoids, embedded within the flexor hallucis brevis mechanism, are integral to the injured complex, so their position and integrity guide grading and management.
additionalDifferentials: Gout of the first MTP joint
Hallux rigidus or first MTP osteoarthritis
Metatarsophalangeal sprain of a lesser toe
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing radiographs including assessment of sesamoid position, with comparison views
MRI to characterise plantar plate, sesamoid and capsular injury
Clinical assessment of first MTP stability and range of movement
Ultrasound in some settings to assess the plantar plate
Bone scan or CT where an occult sesamoid fracture is suspected
redFlags: Gross instability or dislocation of the first MTP joint
Sesamoid diastasis, retraction or fracture suggesting complete plantar plate rupture
Inability to push off or bear weight
Failure to improve, risking chronic instability and deformity
reference.prognosis: Low-grade sprains generally recover with protected rehabilitation over weeks, whereas high-grade injuries with plantar plate rupture or sesamoid disruption may need surgery and can cause prolonged loss of play and long-term stiffness or deformity.
pitfalls: Underestimating a high-grade injury and returning to play too soon
Missing a sesamoid fracture, diastasis or plantar plate rupture
Overlooking progression to hallux rigidus or deformity
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Initial rest, ice, compression, elevation and relative offloading with protected weight-bearing for the acute injury
Immobilisation in stiff-soled footwear, turf-toe taping or a rigid orthosis to limit painful hallux dorsiflexion
Analgesia and anti-inflammatory measures for pain and swelling
Graded rehabilitation restoring first metatarsophalangeal range of movement and strength before return to sport
Grading-based management, with surgical repair reserved for high-grade injuries involving plantar-plate rupture, sesamoid fracture, diastasis or joint instability
Imaging-guided assessment of sesamoid position and joint stability to direct treatment
Sports-medicine and, where indicated, orthopaedic foot-and-ankle referral
